newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew plucks satellite from space.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew plucks satellite from space.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Columbia used its long robotic arm to pluck a prototype satellite factory from space on Monday after swooping past a second satellite orbiting nearby.
"Wake Shield is grappled," astronaut Tamara Jernigan said after the grapple on the end of the 50-foot (17-metre) arm reached out and grabbed the satellite at 9:01 p.m. EST (0201 GMT on Tuesday).
The astronauts then turned off systems on Wake Shield before Jernigan lowered the robot arm to stash the satellite in Columbia's cargo bay about 220 miles (350 km) above South America.

Retrieval of the Wake Shield Facility had been moved up by about three hours from the original schedule so the Orfeus-Spas telescope, an orbiting observatory also deployed by Columbia, would not stray too close to it, NASA officials said.

NASA had never before flown the shuttle in formation with two recoverable satellites. But NASA officials said everything went according to plan during the complicated rendezvous and retrieval Monday night.

Wake Shield was about 16 miles (26 km) from Orfeus-Spas when Columbia swooped between them and retrieved the stainless steel disk 12 feet (4 metres) in diameter. NASA had said they had to be separated by 12.5 miles (20 km) for a safe operation.
"Congratulations on a flawless rendezvous and a great capture of the Wake Shield satellite," spacecraft communicator Marc Garneau told the crew, now more than one-third through its 16-day mission.

Jeff Bantle, mission operations director, told a news conference after the retrieval that the shuttle's satellite communications were briefly interrupted shortly before the retrieval because of a computer problem on the ground.
But he said the problem would not have affected the retrieval even if it had continued.

When the Columbia's five member crew woke up on Monday, they were 23 miles (37 km) ahead of Wake Shield, which Columbia had released on Friday night. The crew moved the orbiter closer to the satellite during the day by firing Columbia's manoeuvring jets as the two craft circled far from Earth.

Earlier on Monday, flight officials congratulated astronaut Story Musgrave, 61, on exceeding 1,000 hours in space. Musgrave, the oldest person to fly in space, was making his sixth and probably last shuttle flight.
"We just made a beautiful pass over Hawaii. The islands are clear today. No matter how many hours you've got up here, these ones are just as good as the first ones," Musgrave said.

NASA believes the two satellites drew unexpectedly close when the Orfeus-Spas telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up as it was pointed at its celestial targets.
The telescope had ceased observations on Sunday so it could be turned to reduce the atmosphere's braking effect on it. It resumed its activities at about 5 a.m. EST (1000 GMT) on Monday.

Wake Shield was designed to manufacture ultra-pure thin film wafers used to make semiconductors for the electronics industry. They could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones.

NASA officials said they were very pleased with the performance of the space factory during the three days it spent orbiting apart from Columbia. Two earlier Wake Shield missions, in 1994 and 1995, had only mixed success.
"I'm elated," Alex Ignatiev, Wake Shield Facility programme director, told the news conference. "It's a great feeling to have an extremely successful flight."

On Wednesday the crew plans to deploy the Wake Shield Facility on the end of the robot arm for another film "growth," after which it will be stashed in Columbia's cargo bay until the spacecraft returns to Earth.

About $29 million has been invested in the Wake Shield project, excluding the costs of each launch. Officials involved with the project said they hoped to send the satellite into space several more times.
